contexts: three hospitals, 38 inpatient wards, one prescribing system
reading: Alert volume trains prescribers to override, so high-severity alerts are lost among low-value ones. Tiering removes interruptions for moderate and minor interactions, which should raise attention to the few that remain, but shifts the risk of moderate interactions onto passive notes and pharmacist surveillance. Because the display is a ward setting and prescribers rotate, the unit of randomisation is the ward, and contamination through rotating prescribers will dilute any difference.

nodes.label: Appropriate response to high-severity alerts
nodes.detail: Accepted or appropriately overridden (claims c1, c4).

nodes.label: Harm from suppressed moderate interactions
nodes.detail: Balancing outcome by pharmacist surveillance (claim c3).

nodes.label: Adverse drug events
nodes.detail: No study shows an effect (claim c5).

summary: Map links alert volume to lost attention and places ward randomisation and harm surveillance around the tiered display.
